title: What would make an AI-native game actually feel fun instead of just impressive?
author: Fearless_Shift7108
selftext:
I’ve been thinking a lot about AI-native games lately, especially the difference between something that looks impressive for a few seconds and something people would actually want to play.

A lot of AI game experiments feel cool at first, but after a minute they can start to feel more like tech demos than real games. I’m curious what people here think would make AI-driven gameplay genuinely fun.

For example, would AI be more useful for dynamic NPCs, branching story choices, world generation, faster prototyping, personalized levels, or something else entirely?

And on the other side, what makes an AI game immediately feel gimmicky or shallow to you?

I’m especially interested in the player experience side of this — not just how AI can generate assets, but what would make the actual gameplay loop feel worth coming back to.

comments.author: fued
comments.body:
the other 95% of game development.

AI just does the initial 5%, the base/content. most of gamedev is playtesting and polish.

replies.author: Aesthetic-Engine
replies.body: There is a good degree of playtesting AI can do for you at this point with the right tools but yeah getting the *feel* right is something it's not advanced enough to weigh in on.

replies.author: Fearless_Shift7108
replies.body: Yeah, this is the part I keep coming back to. AI can get you to a playable thing faster, but the actual fun still seems to come from tuning the loop, watching people play, and cutting the parts that only looked cool in a demo.

comments.author: angrylittledev
comments.body: AI is just the tool, what you do with it is what will limit how your game looks like, feels like and plays like. If you make something basic, demo like, then that's on you, not on AI. AI speeds up what you already have, it's a multiplier. If you have 10 ideas it's up to you to polish them and work them into your game properly. AI is there just to save you time.

comments.author: AsianAnomal
comments.body:
Imo any game that focuses itself around a tool will feel gimicky towards that tool.

Imagine developers doubled down on ray traced graphics to make pixel perfect reflections part of the main game design. Sure itll be cool, and surely you could do some very cool things. But if thats what youre going to base a whole game on, it will get dull fast. I dont buy a game because they use RTX in a unique way, i get the game for what it truly is and RTX can elevate the game

comments.author: EnumeratedArray
comments.body:
Not a great answer to the question, but the game just needs to be fun!

AI doesn't understand what makes a game fun. Most game developers only understand this to an extent. You need to be building with an idea in mind that at least you think is fun and enjoy to play whilst building it, whether AI is used or not.

If you do that, some other people should also find it fun, and then you iterate on it with the community and play testing to find something that is truly fun.

AI can't help with that.

comments.author: SamMakesCode
comments.body:
Games are, fundamentally, an art form. They’re an expression of ideas and emotions. Like all art, you need to think about it in terms of what you’re trying to put out into the world.

If it’s not fun, it might be because AI doesn’t know what fun is. You might be able to use AI as a tool, but it can only produce an average of human ideas.

replies.author: shlaifu
replies.body: ... which is why games are not an artform, at least,not like any of the other arts, in that an average of human ideas might actually be a very good game. Games are amazingly resistant to novelty because novelty of ideas does not factor into gameplay at all. An average of human ideas might still be a very fun game

comments.author: M4xs0n
comments.body: AI isn’t anything you should build your game around. It’s just another component to the other 95% of your game / Game Development

comments.author: 0bscuris
comments.body:
I totally agree with you. I think people have been trying to use ai in nonnovel ways too much. Indie game dev has had asset flip shit forever, it’s the same thing driving alot of disbelief in ai is that they r making essentially ai asset flips.

The real innovation will come from when people stop trying to use the tool to make the same thing but faster, and start looking at what llm does that traditional code can’t. Also, game devs and programmers are control freaks, they don’t like llm being so wild and hard to control, so they throttle it too hard to force consistency, that is a mistake. It’s inconsistency is it’s biggest advantage.

I think the first thing to look at is input. That is the real revolution in what llm does is convert human speech to computer input very well. If ur not looking at ur games input and going ok, how can i make this feel super natural? 

Like, for example, if you take a game like an old turn based jrpg. When you play the game u spend alot of time clicking through menu’s to tell ur team what to do. That should go away immediately. You should just be telling them like you would tell a teammate in real life, which means saying it conversationally instead of an exact string that traditional code demands.

replies.author: Fearless_Shift7108
replies.body: The input point is super interesting. I agree the exciting part isn’t just making old systems faster, it’s letting players express intent more naturally. A party-based RPG where you talk to your team instead of clicking through menus feels way more “AI-native” than just generating more content.

replies.author: 0bscuris
replies.body:
That is the real power of ai, it conversationally converts human thought to computer.

Some of the most fun i’ve had with ai is just giving it some rules around how spells work and then saying, ok as the player, i’m going to invent all the spells in my spell book as i’m playing the game and just freely inventing spells by describing them, the ai checks them against the rules and then just implements them. Right now, it’s just text, but that won’t be forever.

Some other possible uses that do what traditional games can’t:

business sim or political sim, 4x strategy games with actual negotiations with counter parties, video game diplomacy has always sucked, not anymore.

The sims with actual dialogue not just gibberish.

What socom tried to do, first person shooters where ur commanding a team via the mic.

Teammates that can die because they don’t have to be protected for the story to work. Another npc can just fill their role by telling the llm the story beats. “Did you romance garrus? No, he died in the first mission, i romanced xyxy.” A character the player never even met.

comments.author: Savage_PrawnYT
comments.body:
I think I have used Ai kind of creatively for my game. Aside from helping with planning and coding I have also made an Ai backend pipeline that lets players generate infinite monsters, breed and two monsters into brand new species and evolve them over and over. It’s not everyone’s cup of tea but it’s certainly different. Full trailer here if anyone wants to see. Still very early stages tho. 

https://store.steampowered.com/app/4701360/World\_of\_Qreatures/

comments.author: count023
comments.body:
peopel show off how to replicate other games or replicate game functions with AI at a blazing fast pace, but they dont actually mix these things together.

gamedev isn't just "i made an inventory system and a real time combat engine", it's "i'm making a narrative, how do i bend these to my will to achieve that". Expedition 33 coudl be all have done by LLMs potentially and it woudl be fine because it's \_story\_ and it's \_narrative\_ were the appeal, not how well the equipment system or the quest system worked.

comments.author: Shadowlance23
comments.body:
Most AI game dev is being done by people with no programming experience, or understanding of software development. 

Actually writing code is a relatively small part of the process, and that's the only part AI can really do. If you can't write a good story, or design good levels, get player feedback, or any of the dozens of other steps in game design, your game is not going to be good and AI can't help with that.

I could pick up and play the same guitar Jimmy Hendrix played, but I guarantee it won't sound the same.

replies.author: AgenticGameDev
replies.body: Depends on the game but agree in most part. But a more system heavy game would benefit more compared to a puzzle platformer…

comments.author: AutomaticTalent
comments.body:
Having worked a LOT on Lode Runner and been in the room when Tetris was pitched - if at its core it’s fun to do repeatedly at the base level and is like eating peanuts - you may be on to something. 

You can frost a turd all you want but when you get past the frosting it’s still a turd.

Capturing lightning in a bottle takes more effort than most people think. 

One of my favorite questions to ask designers about game development has been “when did your game come alive, like Frankenstein?”.

It is usually an “aha” moment that is small but memorable.

When I was working with Will Wright on Raid on Bungeling Bay he came in one day and showed me the terrain editor and said “You know driving this little bulldozer around terraforming is almost more fun than the game…”.

That was one of those Frankenstein moments. 

I recently had one when trying to fix the control scheme on my AI-coded game. It suddenly clicked and got fun!

Hopefully your core mechanics are solid and repetitively fun.

replies.author: Fearless_Shift7108
replies.body: I really like the “Frankenstein moment” framing. That tiny point where a mechanic suddenly starts feeling fun is probably the thing AI can’t fake. It can help you explore faster, but someone still has to notice when the game actually comes alive.

replies.author: AutomaticTalent
replies.body: One dev I worked with to try to create my game the "traditional" way put it like this:  we keep trying to make a dime but we always come out with 9 cents...

comments.author: AgenticGameDev
comments.body:
Read Dungeon Crawler Carl. It’s a great book. An AI like that would be interesting. Don’t want to spoil it but the current ”bad” state of AI is not a limitation ;). Just use Grok for dialog and lean in to the madness. 

That could be interesting…

comments.author: NovelFlame_AI
comments.body:
I think AI games start feeling shallow the second the world stops meaningfully reacting to the player.

A lot of demos focus on “look, the AI generated infinite stuff,” but infinite content is not the same thing as meaningful consequence. People remember relationships changing, betrayals, reputation shifts, failed decisions coming back later, unexpected emotional moments, stuff like that. Not just endless procedural output.

The interesting part of AI-native systems to me is less “infinite generation” and more making the player feel like the world is actually adapting around them over time. Which is also way harder to pull off.

replies.author: Fearless_Shift7108
replies.body: Yeah, infinite content by itself doesn’t really solve the problem. What would make me come back is if the world remembers what I did — relationships shift, NPCs react differently, or a bad decision comes back later in a way that feels earned.

comments.author: MakeEmMayhem
comments.body:
I’m working on a game called Make'Em Mayhem, an AI-Native game (you can try it out on steam now!) 

The thing that has felt most promising for us is using AI to create new decision pressure, not just new assets. If the player’s generated character changes team comp incentives, item priorities, or how you read a run, then AI is affecting strategy instead of acting like a slot machine for flavor text. 

The stuff that feels gimmicky to me is when the model output is the payoff by itself. The stuff that feels game-like is when the output forces the player to adapt and solve. 

That’s the bar we’ve been using internally: does the AI create a better ‘what do I do with this run?’ question?
